title: What is Rurban Living? Organo Antharam in Hyderabad
paragraphs: Organo Antharam by Organo Eco Habitats is a net-zero residential community in Chevella, Hyderabad, designed around the idea of clusters.

Here, farms grow your food right outside your balcony, and a well-equipped gym is just a short stroll away. You can walk along a stream that flows through the property or take a dip in a bio pool. A luxurious co-working space surrounded by nature helps you focus on work, after which you can return to a spacious villa designed to maximise natural sunlight, fresh air and much more.
This is what Rurban living represents: the simplicity and togetherness of village life, complemented by the comforts of the city.

But the heart of Organo Antharam is Sapthapatha, its Seven Strands of Sustainability, which places healthy food and mindful living at the centre of the community. A goshala with A2 Gir cows, a farm store and a community kitchen bring residents closer to the food they eat and the people they share it with.

title: Indian startup can help you lay home foundation in just one day and without digging
paragraphs: What if your home’s foundation could be built in just one day?
Meet PEN (Pre-Engineered Nail) Foundation by cdisc_technologies_pvt.ltd , an innovative soil-nailing foundation system that can be used to build homes, resorts, offices, and more, almost anywhere.

Here’s the problem: conventional foundations rely on extensive excavation, large quantities of concrete, and intensive site preparation. But even though buildings have evolved, foundation techniques haven’t changed much.

But PEN Foundation is changing that. It uses 80%+ less concrete, delivers up to 70% lower carbon emissions, requires minimal excavation and site disturbance, and helps preserve the topsoil. Each PEN unit can be installed in around two hours, which means the foundation of a standard home can be completed in just one day.

The technology was developed in collaboration with NIT Calicut, IIT Kanpur, and NABL-accredited laboratories. It has also been certified by the GRIHA Council and is positioned as a new approach to low-carbon and sustainable foundation technology in India.

PEN Foundation represents a new way of thinking about construction technology, green buildings, soil conservation, and low-carbon infrastructure, proving that a building can be designed sustainably, right from its foundation.

title: India has a high fever and El Nino is to blame
paragraphs: They are calling it the "Godzilla" El Niño. It is set to peak in December and lead to above-average temperatures across large parts of the world, including India.
Many states, including Maharashtra and Karnataka, have declared drought, with Maharashtra imposing a 10% water cut in many of its districts.
But what is El Niño? And how can we be prepared?

title: Indian startup turns plastic waste into wood - unWOOD
paragraphs: What if the future of wood didn’t need trees?

unWOOD is using physics to rethink what plastic waste can become. Their process combines discarded plastic with earth minerals, changing the material at a molecular level to create a wood-like material that can be worked much like hardwood.

What’s interesting is what this opens up: a material made from waste that can be cut, drilled and used for furniture, while offering properties like waterproofing, termite resistance and weather resistance. Today, that material is being used to make everything from benches and loungers to tables, giving discarded plastic a completely new role.

unWOOD is incubated at NSRCEL-IIMB . They are a part of the Circular Bharat Accelerator, which is a part of Project Circular Bharat, Hindustan Unilever’s flagship plastics circularity program driving India’s transition towards a circular economy.

title: Why Indian men should learn to talk about periods
paragraphs: Periods are normal. So why do we still whisper about them?

Ranu Khade is raising her 10-year-old son, Shaurya, to see periods as normal, not as something gross or embarrassing. Now her team is bringing that lesson to classrooms across India, for girls and boys.Her 10-year-old, Shaurya, knows periods are normal. To him they aren’t embarrassing, they aren’t gross, and they’re nothing to hide. With her team at flawsome, Ranu is now taking that same conversation into schools across India, to boys and girls alike.
Video supported by: Inmyo

title: Inside Bengaluru's Airport Terminal in a Garden - T2
paragraphs: Bengaluru earned its nickname ‘garden city’. At Kempegowda International Airport, this identity got a second life.

The Terminal 2 at blrairport is designed to be more than just a place to catch a flight. Often described as a “terminal in a garden,” the space brings nature into the airport experience through extensive greenery, natural materials, open spaces and biophilic design. But the idea goes beyond aesthetics. The terminal integrates sustainability into its design and operations, showing how large-scale infrastructure can be designed around both people and the environment.
The terminal also celebrates Indian art, traditional crafts and Karnataka’s cultural heritage through its collection of artefacts, installations and handcrafted elements.
Terminal 2 has earned global recognition for its architecture, sustainability and biophilic design, including UNESCO Prix Versailles and Platinum green-building certification

title: This viral truck is driving across North India to deliver sustainability. But at what cost?
paragraphs: Why does a truck need 308 wheels?
This “Baahubali” heavy-haul vehicle is transporting a massive Belgian vessel across India, using hundreds of wheels to distribute an enormous load.
And this load will help turn sugarcane into plastic or PLA.

title: Is bioscience the career of tomorrow? - The Next Gene 2026 by Masters' Union
paragraphs: What if the careers of tomorrow are being created in bioscience today?
At The Next Gene 2026, hosted by Masters' Union , biology meets AI, medicine, technology and entrepreneurship to explore what the next generation of bioscience could look like.

From brain-computer interfaces to new approaches in health and performance, the summit brought together scientists, doctors, founders and students working at the intersection of biology and technology.

But perhaps the most interesting part was seeing how much space there is for young people in this field, through bio-hackathons, startup pitches, workshops and conversations around the problems they could help solve.
As AI becomes increasingly integrated with biology, Bioscience is opening up possibilities far beyond the traditional lab, and creating an entirely new set of careers for the next generation.

title: An Indian startup made a device that can help you detect heart problems without a doctor - Jivascope
paragraphs: JivaScope, a pocket-sized, AI-powered device that enables anyone to self-screen for heart and lung diseases in minutes—bringing clinical-grade diagnostics to rural and low-resource settings.
Jivascope is founded by Tunir Sahoo and Prakarsha De and has also received The James Dyson Award

We came across Jivascope at the The Next Gene 2026 which was Asia's largest hashtag bioscience Summit hosted by Masters' Union. The event bought together students, founders, entrepreneurs along with doctors and scientists in the field of bioscience and biotechnology

title: This place is where India finds out how to turn waste into wealth - IFAT INDIA 2026
paragraphs: IFAT India is India’s largest environmental technology trade fair, focusing on Water Management, Wastewater Treatment, Solid Waste Management, and Recycling Solutions. It serves as a leading platform where sustainable technologies, green innovations, and circular economy solutions are showcased for businesses, startups, and industries aiming to build a cleaner, more conscious future. Here cutting-edge innovations are on display that transform waste into wealth, create green jobs, and enable scalable, sustainable growth across India’s environmental sector.
This year IFAT India is happening at the Bombay Exhibition Centre in Mumbai from the 9-11th sept 2026

title: This company is turning landfills back into landscapes
paragraphs: Zigma Global clears landfill waste and reclaims old dump yards in India using a scientific process called bio-mining.

Government estimates that there are 2,424 dump yard sites in India, holding close to 16 crore tonnes of legacy waste across roughly 15,000 acres. Most of it is land that sits on the city and surrounded by neighbourhoods.
The old fix was capping which was to cover the mound with soil. It’s cheaper, but the waste underneath keeps producing methane and leachate, and the land stays dead.

Zigma has collaborated with Singapore headquartered waste management corporation Blue Planet Environmental Solutions. Waste is excavated and processed to separate materials such as recyclables, organic matter, inert material and Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF).
The RDF can then be used as an alternative fuel in industries such as cement manufacturing, where suitable facilities are equipped to use it.
The other fractions have their own routes. Recovered soil goes into landscaping and levelling low-lying land and recyclables re-enter the material stream.
What’s left at the end is land. Sites that sat for decades leaching into groundwater, catching fire in summer, emitting methane now becomes an open ground that cities can actually use again.

title: An Aadhaar card for garbage - Indian startup builds digital identity system for waste
paragraphs: What if every piece of waste had an Aadhaar?
Green Aadhaar is building a digital identity and traceability system for waste.
Today, a major problem in waste management is not just collection. It is knowing what the waste is, where it goes, and whether it ultimately reaches the right recycling or processing facility.
By creating a digital trail for waste, Green Aadhaar aims to make that journey more transparent and accountable.

And that could have a significant impact. Because when waste can be identified, tracked and traced, its chances of being recovered and recycled can go up dramatically instead of disappearing into mixed waste, landfills or informal disposal chains.

Green Aadhaar is incubated at NSRCEL. They are a part of the Circular Bharat Accelerator, which is a part of Project Circular Bharat, Hindustan Unilever’s flagship plastics circularity program driving India’s transition towards a circular economy.

title: Indian startup makes walls out of recycled paper - HEDRAD
paragraphs: We’ve spent centuries building our homes and offices with brick, concrete and steel. But what if one of the materials shaping the future of construction is something as simple as recycled paper.

That’s the idea behind Hedrad India Founded by Sangeetha Menon, the company makes construction panels that rethink how walls and other building components can be made. Built around a honeycomb-inspired design, the panels offer a lightweight alternative to tradtional construction while helping reduce the time and labour required to put up a structure. The material might sound unconventional, but the technology behind it has undergone testing and received multiple certifications, demonstrating its suitability for use as a construction material.
At a time when we need to rethink not just how much we build, but also what we build with, innovations like these open up new possibilities for materials we may have otherwise considered waste.
This story is supported by Amwoodo which is striving to create a green and plastic-free future.

title: Sustainability meets slow living in Hyderabad - Organo
paragraphs: Where modern living meets the slower rhythm of village life.

Rurban, a blend of “rural” and “urban”, is the idea behind Organo rurbanliving’s modern eco-habitats in Hyderabad which is bringing together the conveniences of modern living with the principles of traditional Indian life. Their communities are built around farms, natural landscapes and walkable neighbourhoods, while the homes draw from Indian architectural elements that have long kept people connected to light, air and nature.

But the idea goes beyond how a home looks. Organo’s Saptapatha framework is also known as the seven strands of sustainability, where every strand is built to bring responsible impact to an interconnected ecosystem. That means locally grown food, community kitchens, employment for surrounding villages, and the everyday infrastructure needed to make sustainable living practical and not just aspirational.
Because perhaps living sustainably isn’t about going back to the past. It’s about understanding what worked then, and designing it for the way we live today.

title: CNG scooter vs EV Scooter - TVS Jupiter CNG /Hybrid - The world's first CNG scooter
paragraphs: What if the future of scooters isn’t electric?

TVS showcased the Jupiter CNG at the last auto expo. It’s the world’s first compressed natural gas scooter, as a possible new direction for cleaner urban mobility. It runs on both, CNG and petrol, allowing riders to switch between the two based on availability.

CNG generally produces lower emissions than petrol and can offer lower running costs, making it a potentially cleaner and more economical option for everyday commuting. Unlike an EV, the scooter doesn’t need to be plugged in or rely entirely on battery-charging infrastructure, while still offering an alternative to conventional petrol-powered mobility.

This positions CNG as an interesting middle ground between petrol and EVs, combining the familiar refuelling experience of a conventional vehicle with the potential for lower emissions and operating costs.

title: Making drinking water free of microplastics, pesticides and uranium
paragraphs: Clear water doesn’t necessarily mean clean water.

Microplastics, uranium and forever chemicals can all be present in water without changing its colour, taste or appearance. As the quality of our water sources changes, purification has to keep up with what’s making its way into them.

LIVPURE is addressing this with its ClearDrop Technology. This is a 10-stage proprietary filtration system designed to target and remove these modern contaminants by almost 99%. But cleaner water is only one part of the challenge. Traditional RO systems can also waste a significant amount of water during purification. Livpure’s high-recovery technology helps reduce the water that gets discarded in the process.

And then there’s what happens after you bring the purifier home. Livpure provides free service and filter changes for a 3 year period. Because the future of water purification isn’t just about making water look clear. It’s about understanding what’s in it, removing what shouldn’t be there, and doing it without wasting the resource we’re trying to protect.

title: Hyderabad startup is using AI to get you fit and healthy at home - PORTL
paragraphs: India’s fitness industry is changing. Our cities are leaving us with less time, more traffic and increasingly less motivation to commute to a gym. That’s why smart home fitness is becoming one of the biggest shifts in the industry. Instead of buying multiple machines or paying for a gym membership, what if one device could bring an entire connected gym into your home?
That’s where Portl fitness comes in.

Portl is backed by t-hubHyd connected to the larger technology and entrepreneurship ecosystem - and they’re building what could be the future of home fitness.They’re building smart fitness systems that combine strength training, cardio, guided workouts and real-time performance tracking, essentially turning a small space at home into a personalised gym.

And the interesting part is the technology. Portl uses AI and connected hardware to make workouts more personalised, track performance and help users train without needing a personal trainer standing beside them.
The future of fitness might not be another gym. It might be the gym that fits inside your home.

title: This city in Tamil Nadu is using roads to save water instead of wasting it
paragraphs: Using roads to store rainwater.
Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu is turning its roads into rainwater-harvesting systems with Eco Bloc technology.
Made from recycled plastic, these underground structures capture and filter rainwater instead of letting it become runoff.
At Race Course Road, Eco Bloc infiltration tanks were built alongside stormwater drains to reduce flooding and recharge groundwater.
Now, the city has proposed scaling the technology to 100 locations, with a ₹100-crore project.

title: Engineer builds a forest on a terrace in the middle of Bengaluru city
paragraphs: This story is supported by Amwoodo which is striving to create a green and plastic-free future.

Venkataraman K turned his terrace in the busy Malleshwaram, Bengaluru into a thriving forest. Today, it’s home to dense greenery, birds, butterflies, and a cooler microclimate proving you don’t need acres of land to bring nature back. When engineered right, a terrace becomes a thriving ecosystem.
His terrace forest is inspired by the western ghats and has three levels of flora and fauna.
